clue.text: Apple mixture English expert put together?

parts.note: Pom is Australian slang for an English person
an ace is an expert or star performer

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether an English specialist assembled a fruity concoction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Apple mixture' reads like a recipe, but it is the pulp left after apples are crushed for cider. POM is Australian and New Zealand slang for an English person.
explanation.definitionFit: Pomace is the crushed pulp of apples, the mash pressed to extract juice for cider.

clue.text: Clergyman's work includes performing rites

indicators.note: the word for work takes the other letters inside it

parts.note: to ply is to work at a trade

indicators.note: performing suggests acting out, so these letters are worked into a new order

explanation.surface: A minister's labours involve carrying out ceremonies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clergyman's' is possessive, so it defines an adjective, not a person. 'performing' is the anagram signal, and 'includes' has the word for work go round the result.
explanation.definitionFit: Priestly means belonging to or befitting a cleric, as a clergyman's duties would be.

clue.text: In horses, frenzied excitement leads to endless anxiety

parts.note: must, or musth, is the frenzied state of a male elephant in rut, and it leads, coming first

indicators.note: without its end the word loses its final letter

parts.note: angst is a feeling of dread or anxiety

explanation.surface: Among horses, wild agitation turns into constant nervousness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endless' drops the T of ANGST. MUST is the frenzy of a rutting elephant, a crossword favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: Mustangs are the feral horses of the American West.

clue.text: US state hasn't severed viable link

indicators.note: a state that has not got a piece has had it taken away

parts.note: Connecticut is a state in New England
severed means cut
on means feasible, as in 'that's not on'

explanation.surface: An American state has not broken off a workable connection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hasn't' removes CUT (severed) from CONNECTICUT, leaving CONNECTI, and ON is added.
explanation.definitionFit: A connection is a tie or relationship joining two things, which is what a link is.

clue.text: Dumpier person carrying out illegal occupation

explanation.surface: A rather stout figure is caught living somewhere unlawfully.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition plays on 'occupation': not a job but occupying a building without the owner's permission.
explanation.definitionFit: Squat describes a short thickset build, so dumpier is its comparative; and someone living in an empty property without right is a squatter.

clue.text: Accommodation housing second team members on

indicators.note: housing means holding inside, so one word goes within the other

parts.note: quarters are lodgings or accommodation
to second a proposal is to back it

explanation.surface: Lodgings are home to the reserve side's players.
explanation.walkthrough: 'second' looks like a number, but it is the verb meaning support. 'on' only joins the surface: these players are on an American football team.
explanation.definitionFit: Quarterbacks are American football players who direct the offence, so they are members of a team.

clue.text: A sailor's spoken of as war hero

indicators.note: something spoken of is said out loud, so the clue words are heard rather than read

parts.note: a jack, or jack tar, is a sailor; with the possessive this sounds like a jacks

explanation.surface: A seaman is described as a hero of battle.
explanation.walkthrough: Say 'a jack's' (a sailor's) out loud. Ajax was a Greek warrior at Troy.
explanation.definitionFit: Ajax was one of the mightiest Greek champions in Homer's account of the Trojan War.

clue.text: Sound of foxy lady

indicators.note: the sound of a word is how it is heard, so the synonym is said out loud

parts.note: foxy means cunning or tricksy

explanation.surface: A seductive woman is heard approaching.
explanation.walkthrough: 'foxy lady' reads as an attractive woman, but 'foxy' means crafty here: TRICKSY, said aloud, gives a woman's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Trixie is a woman's first name, so it names a female person.

clue.text: Singers Jim and Martha split up about start of eighties

indicators.note: about means around, so the outer word goes round the inner letter
in a down entry up means the word is read from the bottom upward

parts.note: to sever is to split or cut apart

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Two singers part company around the dawn of the 1980s.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns SEVER into REVES, and 'about' wraps that round E, the first letter of 'eighties'. 'split up' looks like one phrase about separating.
explanation.definitionFit: Jim Reeves was a country singer and Martha Reeves led the Vandellas, so both share the surname.

clue.text: Barking canines running wild after lead's removed

indicators.note: dogs running wild scatter in all directions, so the remaining letters are thrown into a new order
the leading letter of the word canines is taken off before the shuffle, like a dog let off its lead

explanation.surface: Dogs off the leash tear about madly, making a din.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barking' looks like dog noise to fit the canines, but it means mad. 'lead's removed' drops the C of CANINES, leaving ANINES, and 'running wild' rearranges those letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Barking, short for barking mad, is British slang for crazy, the same as mentally unhinged.

clue.text: Find mother briefly looking at European periodical

parts.note: ma is an informal word for mother

indicators.note: said briefly, the word for looking loses its final letter

parts.note: gazing means looking steadily

explanation.surface: Someone spots their mother glancing at a continental journal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'briefly' cuts the last letter from GAZING, leaving GAZIN. 'Find' does no work in the wordplay and joins the surface only.
explanation.definitionFit: A magazine is a publication issued at regular intervals, which is what a periodical is.

clue.text: 17th century ruler, say, a man of many parts

indicators.note: say marks a word as spoken, so the name is heard not seen

parts.note: James Stuart was the name of the Stuart kings James I and James II

explanation.surface: A Stuart monarch is described as a versatile fellow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a man of many parts' sounds like a versatile person but means an actor with many roles: James Stewart, Hollywood star. The Stuart kings James I and II reigned in the 1600s.
explanation.definitionFit: James Stewart was the Hollywood actor who played roles across a long film career, so many parts.

clue.text: Accessories locked in box with flexible strap

annotationWithheld.why: 'Accessories locked in box with flexible strap' as held gives SPAR (box) and PARTS (anagram of strap) but no word for the E of SPARE; a word seems lost in OCR.
annotationWithheld.clue: Accessories locked in box with flexible strap

clue.text: Prefer, as it were

definitions.meaning: to favour or have a taste for something
a filler phrase meaning so to speak, the conversational filler used in casual speech

explanation.surface: Two short phrases about choosing and qualifying a remark.
explanation.definitionFit: To prefer something is to be fond of it; and the casual filler word sprinkled into speech serves as a hedge, so to speak.

clue.text: Send back meal ticket

parts.note: to return something is to send it back
fare is food, the meal provided

explanation.surface: A diner rejects the meal voucher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Send back meal' reads as a diner complaining, but the pieces join to a kind of travel ticket.
explanation.definitionFit: A return fare is the price of a trip there and back, and so a ticket type.

clue.text: Debonair sort the girl hated

indicators.note: to sort things is to rearrange them into order, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A suave type was loathed by a particular young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Debonair sort' looks like a phrase describing a man, but 'sort' is the anagram signal working on THE GIRL HATED.
explanation.definitionFit: Debonair can mean carefree and cheerful, which is the sense of being free of worry.

clue.text: Direct path of vehicle northwards on AI and get lost

indicators.note: in a down entry going northwards means reading from the bottom up

parts.note: a van is a vehicle

indicators.note: something lost has gone astray, so the letters wander into a new order

explanation.surface: A driver heads north on the A1 and gets lost while trying to steer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'northwards' turns VAN into NAV; 'lost' rearranges AI and GET into IGATE. The surface's A1 is Britain's main north-south road.
explanation.definitionFit: To navigate is to plan and steer a course, choosing the route to take.

clue.text: Lens, say, through which you once spotted girl

indicators.note: one piece passes through the other, so it sits inside it

parts.note: say introduces an example, abbreviated eg
ye is the old form of you
a lass is a girl

explanation.surface: An old monocle through which a man once ogled a young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lens, say' looks like one phrase, but 'say' is EG, with YE (old 'you') through it. 'spotted' joins the surface only.
explanation.definitionFit: An eyeglass is a single lens or monocle worn to help sight.

clue.text: Wrongdoers banned by US city's railway station staff

parts.note: cons is slang for convicts
tabu is a variant spelling of taboo, meaning forbidden
LA is Los Angeles

explanation.surface: Criminals are barred by rail staff at an American city's station.
explanation.walkthrough: 'station staff' suggests railway workers, given 'railway' in the clue, but the station is a police station.
explanation.definitionFit: A constabulary is a police force, the officers who staff a police station.

clue.text: Island welcome received by film director

indicators.note: received by means taken inside, so one word holds the other

parts.note: Jacques Tati was a French film director, maker of Monsieur Hulot's Holiday
hi is a word of greeting or welcome

explanation.surface: A film-maker gives a warm greeting to an island.
explanation.walkthrough: Jacques Tati is a French comic film director often used in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: Tahiti is the largest of the Society Islands in French Polynesia.

clue.text: Vitamin — small quantity — for vitality

parts.note: B is a vitamin group
an ounce is a small amount

explanation.surface: A little vitamin supplement gives you energy.
explanation.walkthrough: Vitamins are named by letters, so 'Vitamin' gives B.
explanation.definitionFit: Bounce means liveliness and energy, as in a spring in one's step.

clue.text: Nothing in a manuscript contributing to book

indicators.note: in places the zero within the letters for the manuscript

parts.note: nothing is zero, shaped like the letter O

explanation.surface: A blank space in a handwritten text makes its way into a volume.
explanation.walkthrough: The book is one of the Old Testament prophets.
explanation.definitionFit: Amos is a book of the Old Testament, named after the prophet.

clue.text: Former radio show's disappointing finale for Stuck? Then call our solutions li Service supplied by ATS, PO Box 78 listeners

indicators.note: what listeners take in is the sound, so the phrase is heard rather than read

parts.note: a feeble conclusion is a weak ending

explanation.surface: An old wireless comedy is said to end on a flat note.
explanation.walkthrough: The held text has a solving-line advert ('Stuck? Then call our solutions li Service supplied by ATS, PO Box 78') merged in by OCR; the clue is 'Former radio show's disappointing finale for listeners'. Week Ending was a BBC Radio 4 satirical sketch show.
explanation.definitionFit: Week Ending was a long-running BBC radio comedy of topical sketches, now ended, so a former programme.

clue.text: Father has met a posh German woman

parts.note: Fr is the abbreviation for Father, a priest's title
U means upper-class, as in U and non-U

explanation.surface: A priest meets an upper-class lady from Germany.
explanation.walkthrough: U for upper-class comes from the 'U and non-U' classification of British speech.
explanation.definitionFit: Frau is the German title for a married woman, like Mrs.

clue.text: Dinner manifestly more than enough for me?

indicators.note: the clue words hold more letters than needed, so the answer is a stretch found within them

explanation.surface: A diner suspects the meal served is obviously too big for them.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits inside 'Dinner manifestly'. The surface is apt: a large dinner satisfies one's appetite, the self that wants feeding.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means one's inner self or soul, humorously one's stomach, so the speaker's own being.

clue.text: Guerrilla leader found way to exterminate a group of reservists

parts.note: to zap is to kill or destroy quickly
TA is the Territorial Army, Britain's volunteer reserve force

explanation.surface: A rebel chief devises a method of wiping out a unit of part-time soldiers.
explanation.walkthrough: Emiliano Zapata led peasant guerrillas in the Mexican Revolution. The TA, Territorial Army, was the British Army's volunteer reserve.
explanation.definitionFit: Emiliano Zapata was the revolutionary commander of peasant fighters in southern Mexico.

clue.text: Card-carrying actors are, and it's not fair

definitions.meaning: actors holding a union card belong to Equity, the British performers' trade union, so they are members of it
something unjust, a lack of fairness

explanation.surface: Union members on stage complain about an injustice.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the first part as two words, IN EQUITY: Equity is the actors' union in Britain, so union members are in it.
explanation.definitionFit: Inequity is injustice or unfairness; and actors with a union card are members of the performers' union, split as two words.

clue.text: Stones, No I for the French and some Britons (though not quite all)

parts.note: je is French for I

indicators.note: not quite all of the word is used, so its last letter is dropped

parts.note: the Welsh are some of the peoples of Britain

explanation.surface: Gems are linked to a French speaker and to a few Britons, though not every one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not quite all' cuts the H from WELSH, leaving WELS. 'No' plays no part in the wordplay and is likely an OCR stray.
explanation.definitionFit: Jewels are precious stones, the gems set in rings and crowns.
